pos: n. (the Styrian Benedictine abbey of 1074, holding the largest monastic library in the world)
etymology: Latin Ad montes, at the mountains, from the abbey's situation in the Enns valley.
biblical_def: Admont in Styria was founded in 1074 by Archbishop Gebhard of Salzburg out of a bequest of St Hemma of Gurk, and has been inhabited by Benedictines ever since. Its library hall, finished in 1776, is the largest monastic library room in the world: two hundred and thirty feet long, seven cupolas painted by Bartolomeo Altomonte, and some seventy thousand volumes on the shelves out of two hundred thousand in the abbey's keeping, including the twelfth-century Admont Giant Bible. The rest of the monastery burned in 1865 and was rebuilt; the library was saved. The dictionary records Admont because a room of that size makes an unavoidable point about rank. Among two hundred thousand books one claims an origin the others do not, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), and the sanctifying work is assigned to that one, “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17). It is also the book meant for readers with no shelf of their own, “The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130), and the one against which the other hundred and ninety-nine thousand are to be measured, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a library as a collection of books; a codex is a manuscript volume; a manuscript as a book written by hand; a cupola as a spherical vault on the top of a building; and a folio as a book of the largest size.
webster_full: LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution.
MANUSCRIPT, n. A book or paper written with the hand or pen; a writing, in distinction from a printed copy.
VELLUM, n. A finer kind of parchment or skin, dressed and prepared for writing.
CUPOLA, n. In architecture, a spherical vault on the top of an edifice; a dome.
FOLIO, n. A book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet of paper.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Styrian Benedictine abbey of 1074 whose library hall is the largest monastic library room in the world.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a vast library needs a ranked shelf. Admont keeps two hundred thousand volumes, and exactly one of them makes a claim about its own origin, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16).

The live temptation is a learning that flattens its sources, so that the inspired book becomes a specimen among specimens in a very beautiful room. Scripture assigns the sanctifying office to itself and not to the collection, “thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17); it is addressed to readers who own nothing, “it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130); and it offers itself as the measure of everything else on the shelves, “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

pos: n. (the Upper Austrian Benedictine abbey of 777, keeping the Tassilo Chalice and an eighteenth-century observatory tower)
etymology: German Kremsmunster, the minster on the Krems, from Munster, a monastery church.
biblical_def: Kremsmunster in Upper Austria was founded in 777 by Tassilo III, duke of Bavaria, by tradition in memory of his son Gunther, killed by a boar while hunting in the valley. It keeps the Tassilo Chalice, a gilt copper cup of about 780 that is among the most important surviving objects of the Carolingian age, and the Codex Millenarius, an eighth-century gospel book. Between 1749 and 1758 the abbey built the Mathematical Tower, eight storeys of cabinets of natural history, physics and astronomy with an observatory on top, one of the earliest such towers in Europe. The dictionary records Kremsmunster for that tower, because it is a monastery taking the created order seriously, and for the order of knowing that Scripture insists on. Study begins with a disposition and not with an instrument, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10), and the understanding it yields is tested in obedience, “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments” (Psa 111:10). The failure mode of a learned institution is the one Nebuchadnezzar demonstrates on his own roof, “that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power” (Dan 4:30), and God states beforehand that He will not share the credit, “my glory will I not give to another” (Isa 42:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an observatory as a place for observing the heavenly bodies; a chalice as a cup or bowl; astronomy as the science of the heavenly bodies; a cabinet in this sense as a collection of curiosities; and a minster as a monastery, also a cathedral church.
webster_full: OBSERVATORY, n. A place or building for making observations on the heavenly bodies.
CHALICE, n. A cup or bowl; usually, a communion cup.
ASTRONOMY, n. The science which teaches the knowledge of the celestial bodies, their magnitudes, motions and distances.
CABINET, n. A set of boxes or drawers for curiosities; also, a private room in which consultations are held.
MINSTER, n. A monastery; an ecclesiastical convent or fraternity; also, a cathedral church.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever.

The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?

corruption_summary: Upper Austrian Benedictine abbey of 777 holding the Tassilo Chalice and an eight-storey observatory tower of 1749.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that natural philosophy has a proper home in a Christian house and a proper starting point. Kremsmunster stacked eight storeys of cabinets under an observatory, and the order of knowing is settled before the first instrument is bought, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).

The live temptation is the inversion, where learning becomes the ground of reverence instead of its fruit, and then the credit quietly changes hands. Scripture tests understanding by obedience, “his praise endureth for ever” (Psa 111:10); it records the exact words of a man surveying his own achievement, “Is not this great Babylon” (Dan 4:30); and it reports God's refusal to divide the honour, “I am the LORD: that is my name” (Isa 42:8).

pos: n. (the Lower Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1089 on the Danube, source of the fifteenth-century Melk reform)
etymology: Slavic Medilica, a boundary place, through Old High German Medelike.
biblical_def: Melk stands on a rock over the Danube, where Leopold II of Babenberg gave his castle to Benedictine monks in 1089. In the fifteenth century it became the centre of the Melk reform, a movement that spread through the Austrian and south German houses, restoring the rule where it had lapsed, rebuilding libraries and reforming discipline from the inside without waiting for a pope or a council. Between 1702 and 1746 Jakob Prandtauer rebuilt the whole abbey as the best-known baroque monastery in Europe. The dictionary records Melk for that reform, because self-correction inside an institution is the rarest thing in church history and Scripture requires it by name. The charge laid on a church that has slipped begins with a diagnosis of affection rather than of practice, “because thou hast left thy first love” (Rev 2:4), and the remedy prescribed is a return to what was done at the start, “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5). The prophetic summons is likewise backward before it is forward, “Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts” (Mal 3:7), and the end in view is a church presented clean, “a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle” (Eph 5:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reform as a change from worse to better; discipline as instruction and government; a rule as a prescribed form of conduct; to repent as to feel sorrow for sin with amendment; and a visitation as the act of a superior who inspects.
webster_full: REFORM, v.t. To change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to laws and rules; correction; chastisement.
RULE, n. A prescribed form or standard of conduct or practice; government; sway.
REPENT, v.i. To sorrow or be pained for sin, as a violation of God's holy law, with amendment of life.
VISITATION, n. The act of a superior or superintending officer, who visits a corporation or religious house to inspect.

Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.

Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.

Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. But ye said, Wherein shall we return?
Eph 5:27
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
corruption_summary: Lower Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1089 whose fifteenth-century reform restored the rule across the Austrian and south German houses.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an institution can reform itself from the inside, and that Scripture asks exactly that of a slipping church. Melk did it in the fifteenth century without waiting for Rome, and the diagnosis Christ gives such a house concerns its affections, “Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee” (Rev 2:4).

The live temptation is a reform of discipline that never reaches the heart, which leaves a tidier house and the same disease. The prescribed remedy is deliberately retrospective, “and do the first works” (Rev 2:5); the prophetic call is a turning back before it is a going forward, “Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances” (Mal 3:7); and the end Christ has in view is a bride without blemish rather than an abbey without scandal, “but that it should be holy and without blemish” (Eph 5:27).

pos: n. (the Lower Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1083, called the Austrian Montecassino, with an imperial staircase painted to flatter an emperor)
etymology: German Gottweig, probably God's consecrated place, from Gott and a root for dedication.
biblical_def: Gottweig stands on a hill above the Danube opposite Krems, founded in 1083 by Bishop Altmann of Passau, and from its situation and scale it has long been called the Austrian Montecassino. It burned in 1718 and Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt rebuilt it to a palatial design never wholly finished. Its imperial staircase carries Paul Troger's ceiling of 1739, in which the Emperor Charles VI is painted as Apollo driving the sun, surrounded by the virtues, in the largest baroque stair-hall fresco in Austria. The dictionary records Gottweig for that ceiling, which is a monastery painting a man into the place of a god in order to keep his favour. God states in advance that the arrangement is not available, “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another” (Isa 42:8), and the day appointed against exalted men is announced, “upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low” (Isa 2:12). The royal dignity that Scripture does distribute goes to believers and not to Habsburgs, “And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father” (Rev 1:6), and the preeminence in all things is reserved by name, “that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Col 1:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines flattery as false praise; apotheosis as deification; preeminence as superiority in degree; patronage as support given by a patron; and a fresco as a painting on fresh plaster.
webster_full: FLATTERY, n. False praise; commendation bestowed for the purpose of gaining favor and influence.
APOTHEOSIS, n. Deification; the act of placing a prince or other person among the heathen deities.
PREEMINENCE, n. Superiority in degree, quality or dignity; precedence.
PATRONAGE, n. Special countenance or support; favor, encouragement or aid afforded to a person or a work.
FRESCO, n. A method of painting on walls with water colors, on fresh plaster, or on a wall not yet dry.
scriptures: Isa 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.
Isa 2:12
For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low:
Rev 1:6
And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
corruption_summary: Lower Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1083 whose imperial staircase paints Charles VI as Apollo driving the sun.
corruption_paragraphs: Troger's ceiling at Gottweig puts a living emperor in the chariot of the sun, attended by virtues, on the ceiling of a Benedictine house. Whatever the conventions of baroque allegory, the transaction is plain: the abbey needed Habsburg favour and paid for it in divine imagery. The LORD had already refused the arrangement in advance, “and my glory will I not give to another” (Isa 42:8).

The corruption is not confined to painted ceilings. Any church that borrows the vocabulary of worship to secure the protection of power is doing the same thing in a cheaper medium. Isaiah names the outcome for exalted men, “For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty” (Isa 2:12); the royal standing Scripture actually distributes is given to ordinary believers, “to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever” (Rev 1:6); and the first place is reserved by name for one Person, “And he is the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18).

pos: n. (the Lower Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1112, with a famous garden and a school kept since 1814)
etymology: German Seitenstetten, probably the settlements on the side, from Seite and Stetten.
biblical_def: Seitenstetten in the Mostviertel was founded in 1112 by Udalschalk of Heft and has been held by Benedictines since. It was rebuilt in the eighteenth century by Joseph Munggenast, and it is known for two things besides its church: a garden, laid out as a working ornamental and kitchen garden with hedged compartments and a long pergola, and a secondary school that the abbey has run since 1814 and still runs. The dictionary records Seitenstetten for that combination, a garden and a schoolroom kept by the same house, because Scripture ties settled cultivation and settled teaching to the same promise. The psalmist's charge to a man who wants to stay somewhere is two plain verbs with a consequence, “Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land” (Psa 37:3). Real husbandry requires that a man actually know what he keeps, “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23). The contentment proper to a received portion is confessed, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places” (Psa 16:6), and the law of any garden or any classroom is the same and is not negotiable, “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a garden as a piece of ground appropriated to plants; a pergola is an arbour or covered walk; horticulture as the cultivation of a garden; tillage as the operation of ploughing and preparing ground; and a seminary as a place of education.
webster_full: GARDEN, n. A piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, or plants, fruits and flowers.
ARBOR, n. A frame of lattice work, covered with vines or branches; a bower; a shady retreat.
HORTICULTURE, n. The cultivation of a garden; or the art of cultivating gardens.
TILLAGE, n. The operation, practice or art of tilling or preparing land for seed, and keeping it free from weeds.
SEMINARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university.
scriptures: Psa 37:3

Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.
Psa 16:6
The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
Gal 6:7

corruption_summary: Lower Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1112 keeping a working ornamental garden and a secondary school since 1814.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that cultivation and teaching are the same kind of patience. Seitenstetten has kept a garden and a classroom in the same precinct for two centuries, and the psalmist's charge to anyone who means to stay put is two verbs and a consequence, “so shalt thou dwell in the land” (Psa 37:3).

The live temptation in both trades is a management that stops looking. The proverb requires real knowledge of what is held, “and look well to thy herds” (Pro 27:23); the right disposition toward a received portion is gratitude rather than ambition, “yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psa 16:6); and the law that governs a seed-bed governs a schoolroom, “Be not deceived; God is not mocked” (Gal 6:7).

pos: n. (the Upper Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1056, whose eleventh-century frescoes were found in 1956 beneath later plaster)
etymology: German Lambach, the brook of the Lambach stream, from Bach, a brook.
biblical_def: Lambach on the Traun was founded as a collegiate church by Count Arnold II of Wels-Lambach and converted into a Benedictine abbey in 1056 by his son Adalbero, bishop of Wurzburg. It was rebuilt in baroque, and in 1956 workmen uncovered beneath the later plaster of the west choir a cycle of frescoes painted about 1080: the Magi before Herod, the massacre of the innocents, the flight into Egypt, among the oldest wall paintings in the German-speaking lands and among the best preserved anywhere of their date. They had been covered for five hundred years. The dictionary records Lambach for that recovery, because it is a parable of the Reformation's own method: the older layer was there all along under the fashionable surface. The prophetic instruction is to go and look for it, “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), and the drift that plastered it over is described as a preference for unmarked ground, “to walk in paths, in a way not cast up” (Jer 18:15). The command about inherited boundaries applies to doctrine as much as to fields, “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28), and the honour promised to those who uncover and rebuild is considerable, “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach” (Isa 58:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fresco as a painting on fresh plaster; to whitewash as to cover with a white liquid; plaster as a composition for covering walls; to restore as to bring back to a former state; and antiquity as ancient times.
webster_full: FRESCO, n. A method of painting on walls with water colors, on fresh plaster, or on a wall laid with mortar not yet dry.
WHITEWASH, v.t. To cover with a white liquid, as lime and water; to make white.
PLASTER, n. A composition of lime, water and sand, well mixed, used for coating walls and partitions of buildings.
RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former owner; to bring back; to repair; to renew; to re-establish.
ANTIQUITY, n. Ancient times; former ages; times long since past; also, the remains of ancient times.

Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Because my people hath forgotten me, they have burned incense to vanity, and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up;

corruption_summary: Upper Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1056 whose frescoes of about 1080 lay hidden under plaster for five centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the older layer is usually still there. Lambach's eleventh-century Magi had been plastered over for five hundred years and needed only to be looked for, and the prophet's instruction to a drifting people is phrased as exactly that kind of search, “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths” (Jer 6:16).

The live temptation is the plaster: a generation covers what it does not understand and calls the covering an improvement. Jeremiah names the motion as a turning aside onto unmade roads, “Because my people hath forgotten me” (Jer 18:15); the law about boundaries applies to doctrine as much as to fields, “Remove not the ancient landmark” (Pro 22:28); and the title given to those who dig back down to the footings is honourable, “The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isa 58:12).

pos: n. (the Upper Austrian Benedictine abbey of 748, source of the Mondsee Fragments, the earliest literary texts in German)
etymology: German Mondsee, the moon lake, from Mond and See.
biblical_def: Mondsee in the Salzburg lake district was founded in 748 by Odilo of Bavaria and is one of the oldest monasteries in Austria. Its scriptorium produced, about the year 810, the manuscript known as the Mondsee Fragments: among the earliest literary texts in the German language, including a translation of the Gospel of Matthew and of a sermon of Augustine into Old Bavarian. The abbey was dissolved by Joseph II in 1791 and its church is now a parish church. The dictionary records Mondsee for those fragments, because a monk putting Matthew into the speech of his own village in 810 is doing by instinct what the Reformation would later have to fight for. The text claims to do its work on the untaught, which presupposes that they can read or hear it, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). It is the instrument of sanctifying and therefore must be understood, “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17). Its claim about itself covers the whole of it, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), and the hearers it commends are those who checked what they were told against a copy, “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a scriptorium as a writing-room; a fragment as a part broken off; a version as a translation; Bavarian as pertaining to Bavaria; and a gospel as a history of the birth and life of Christ.
webster_full: SCRIPTORIUM, n. A room in a monastery set apart for writing and copying manuscripts.
FRAGMENT, n. A part broken off; a piece separated from any thing by breaking; an imperfect part.
VERSION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.

scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: Upper Austrian Benedictine abbey of 748 whose scriptorium produced the Mondsee Fragments, the earliest literary German.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that putting Scripture into the common speech is the oldest instinct and not the newest. A Mondsee monk rendered Matthew into Old Bavarian about 810, and the claim the psalmist makes for the text requires that kind of access, “it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).

The live temptation is the one the later medieval church institutionalised against Mondsee's own instinct, a text kept in a language the congregation did not have. Scripture ties sanctifying to a word that must be understood, “thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17); its claim covers every part of itself and not an authorised extract, “and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16); and the hearers it praises had copies in their hands, “they received the word with all readiness of mind” (Act 17:11).

pos: n. (the Salzburg Benedictine nunnery of about 714, the oldest continuously existing convent of women in the German-speaking lands)
etymology: German Nonnberg, the nuns' hill, from Nonne and Berg.
biblical_def: Nonnberg in Salzburg was founded about 714 by Rupert, the city's first bishop, with his kinswoman Erentrudis as first abbess, and Benedictine women have lived there without a break ever since, which makes it the oldest continuously existing convent of women north of the Alps. The church keeps Romanesque frescoes of about 1150 in the nuns' choir and a late Gothic winged altar. The dictionary records Nonnberg for that thirteen-hundred-year continuance, and names the one thing the Reformers asked such houses to give up, which was not the common life but the perpetual vow. Scripture treats a vow as binding the moment it is made, “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it” (Ecc 5:4), and draws the obvious conclusion about rash ones, “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5). Vowing is not forbidden; paying is required, “Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God” (Psa 76:11). What is named as a mark of departing doctrine is making the single life a law, “Forbidding to marry” (1Ti 4:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a nun as a woman devoted to a religious life in a cloister; an abbess as the female superior of a nunnery; a vow as a solemn promise made to God; a postulant is one who petitions for admission; and continence as restraint of the appetites.
webster_full: NUN, n. A woman who devotes herself to a religious life, and lives in a cloister or convent.
ABBESS, n. A female superior or governess of a nunnery or convent of nuns.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; a solemn promise accompanied with a religious sanction.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a covered passage or walk round a court.
CONTINENCE, n. Restraint; a withholding; chastity; forbearance of lawful pleasure.
scriptures: Ecc 5:4
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
Ecc 5:5
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared.
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
corruption_summary: Salzburg Benedictine nunnery of about 714, the oldest continuously existing convent of women north of the Alps.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Reformation struck at the perpetual vow and not at a household of unmarried women. Nonnberg has kept such a household for thirteen centuries, and the preacher's rule about vows is what makes a lifelong one so grave, “pay that which thou hast vowed” (Ecc 5:4).

The live temptation is to treat the vow as the holiness, or else to treat singleness as a defect. Scripture does neither. It warns against the rash promise on plain prudential grounds, “than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5); it commands the paying of vows actually made, “let all that be round about him bring presents unto him” (Psa 76:11); and it lists the prohibition of marriage, not the practice of celibacy, among the marks of departure, “and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3).

pos: n. (the Salzburg Benedictine abbey of about 785, keeping the twelfth-century Walther Bible)
etymology: German Michaelbeuern, Michael's dwellings, from the dedication and Beuern, dwellings.
biblical_def: Michaelbeuern north of Salzburg was founded about 785, probably by the Bavarian Sieghardinger family, and is one of the smallest Benedictine houses still in community, with a dozen or so monks who serve the surrounding parishes. Its treasure is the Walther Bible, a great illuminated two-volume Bible written and painted in the abbey about 1180 by a monk named Walther, who put his own portrait at the end with a note asking the reader to pray for him. The dictionary records Michaelbeuern for that colophon, because a man spending years copying Scripture by hand is the plainest illustration of work offered up. The motive Scripture supplies for such labour is the Lord rather than the reader, “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23), and the prayer that fits a finished work is for its establishing and not its fame, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17). The workman is told what standard he is working to, “a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15), and the reason a decade of vellum is not wasted is the durability of what is written on it, “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colophon as an inscription at the end of a book; illumination as the adorning of a manuscript with colours; vellum as a fine parchment; a scribe as one who writes or copies; and to copy as to write after an original.
webster_full: COLOPHON, n. The conclusion of a book, formerly containing the place and year of publication.
ILLUMINATE, v.t. To adorn with colored pictures or ornamental letters, as a manuscript.
VELLUM, n. A finer kind of parchment or skin, dressed and prepared for writing.
SCRIBE, n. A writer; one who writes or draws up writings; a notary; a copyist.
COPY, v.t. To write, print or engrave, according to an original; to transcribe.
scriptures: Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
corruption_summary: Small Salzburg Benedictine abbey of about 785 keeping the Walther Bible, copied and illuminated there about 1180.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that long unglamorous work has a stated motive. Walther spent years on two volumes of vellum and signed them with a request for prayer, and the apostle supplies the only motive that makes such a decade reasonable, “as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23).

The live temptation is to make the copying itself meritorious, which is how a scriptorium becomes a workshop of merit and a colophon becomes an invoice. Scripture leaves the finished work in God's hands, “yea, the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17); it names the standard a workman answers to, “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15); and it gives the real reason the vellum was worth the years, “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth” (Isa 40:8).

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey at Innsbruck, founded 1138 on the Roman site of Veldidena, with a founding legend of penance)
etymology: Latin Veldidena, the Roman station on the Inn, through Middle High German Wilten.
biblical_def: Wilten in Innsbruck stands on the site of the Roman station of Veldidena and was founded as a Premonstratensian house in 1138, the canons having probably replaced an older community. Its founding legend is told in a wooden figure that still stands in the porch: the giant Haymon, having killed another giant named Thyrsus in a quarrel, is said to have built the abbey as penance for the murder and to have served in it until his death. The present church is a rococo rebuilding of the 1660s and later. The dictionary records Wilten for that legend, because it states the medieval theory of satisfaction in the bluntest possible terms: a man kills, and he builds a church to pay for it. Scripture denies the transaction. The saved are saved by the opposite of works, “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Tit 3:5), and the justified man is described precisely as one who is not working, “But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly” (Rom 4:5). The clause that excludes boasting is placed next to the gift on purpose, “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9), and the satisfaction itself was made once by another and is complete, “For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines penance as pain or suffering voluntarily undergone for sin; satisfaction as payment, that which satisfies a claim; expiation as the act of atoning for a crime; merit as desert, claim to reward; and a canon regular is a clergyman living under a rule.
webster_full: PENANCE, n. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him as a punishment for sin.
SATISFACTION, n. The act of satisfying; payment; amends; atonement for a crime; that which satisfies.
EXPIATION, n. The act of atoning for a crime; the act of making satisfaction for an offense.
MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles to honor or reward.
CANON, n. In the church, a dignitary; a clergyman belonging to a cathedral or collegiate church.
scriptures: Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
corruption_summary: Premonstratensian abbey at Innsbruck, founded 1138 on Roman Veldidena, with a founding legend of a church built as penance for murder.
corruption_paragraphs: The giant Haymon in Wilten's porch is a legend, but the theology in it was taught in earnest. A man commits a murder and builds a church to satisfy for it; the abbey is the payment. That is the doctrine of satisfaction working at village level, and Scripture refuses it at the root, “Not by works of righteousness which we have done” (Tit 3:5).

Rome has not retracted the structure, keeping satisfaction as part of the sacrament of penance and attaching indulgences to pious works. Paul's description of the justified man is deliberately scandalous and leaves the builder nothing to present, “his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5). The clause excluding boasting is set immediately beside the gift to prevent this very mixture, “lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9), and the satisfaction that was required has been made once, by someone else, with nothing outstanding, “For by one offering he hath perfected for ever” (Heb 10:14).
